passages.t: Solomon writes to Hiram of Tyre
passages.happening:
‘Now Solomon purposed to build a house for the Name of the LORD and a royal palace for himself’ (verse 1). He conscripts porters, stonecutters and supervisors (verse 2), and sends word to Hiram king of Tyre to do for him what he did for David (verse 3).

The house is for incense, the showbread and the daily offerings, the worship the law commands (verse 4). ‘The house that I am building will be great, for our God is greater than all gods’ (verse 5). ‘But who is able to build a house for Him, since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain Him?’ (verse 6). Solomon asks for a craftsman skilled in metal and in purple, crimson and blue yarn, and for cedar, cypress and algum from Lebanon, and promises wheat, barley, wine and oil for the woodcutters (verses 7-10).
passages.hearers:
The gift of wisdom in chapter 1 turns into action. The temple David planned moves from plan to building site, and this chapter is the preparation: labor, materials and skill. Chapters 3 and 4 tell the building, and 5 to 7 its dedication.

Tyre was the leading Phoenician city, on an island off the coast of today's Lebanon, the center of a trade network across the Mediterranean. Its king, Hiram, had sent cedar for David's palace. The cedar of Lebanon was prized across the ancient Near East, and rulers of Mesopotamia and Egypt boasted of bringing it home. First Kings 5 tells the same agreement with some differences: there Solomon pays Hiram's household yearly in wheat and oil, here the woodcutters in wheat, barley, wine and oil. The two may describe different parts of the arrangement.

Solomon's letter does theology as well as business. The house will be great because God is great, yet the highest heavens cannot hold him; the phrase is literally the heavens and the heavens of heavens, a Hebrew way of saying the uttermost heights. The worship it describes, incense, showbread renewed each Sabbath, offerings morning and evening, was the worship of the second temple too, the Chronicler's readers' own.
passages.later: At the dedication Solomon will pray the same thought: ‘But will God indeed dwell with man upon the earth?’ (2 Chronicles 6:18). Stephen said, ‘However, the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands’ (Acts 7:48).
passages.asks: Solomon built with all his skill and wealth, and said in the same breath that no house could hold God. Ask whether your work for God holds both: your best effort, and the knowledge that it is never enough to contain him. And ask what in your life is built only for God's name.

passages.t: Hiram's answer, and the labor force
passages.happening:
Hiram writes back: “Because the LORD loves His people, He has set you over them as king” (verse 11). He praises the LORD, ‘who made the heavens and the earth’ (verse 12), for giving David a wise son. He sends Huram-abi, son of a woman of Dan and a man of Tyre, skilled in gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, wood, yarn and fine linen (verses 13-14). His men will cut the logs and float them as rafts by sea to Joppa, and Solomon can take them up to Jerusalem (verse 16).

‘Solomon numbered all the foreign men in the land of Israel following the census his father David had conducted, and there were found to be 153,600 in all’ (verse 17), and he sets them to work as porters, stonecutters and supervisors (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
A foreign king praises the LORD as maker of heaven and earth and names God's love as the reason Israel has a king. The word for love is ahavah. The Chronicler lets an outsider say it.

Huram-abi stood between two peoples, his mother from Dan and his father from Tyre. The Chronicler shapes him as a second Oholiab, the craftsman of Dan who worked on the tabernacle, so that the temple's builders echo the tabernacle's. The purple, crimson and blue yarn were the colors of the tabernacle curtains; Phoenician purple dye, made at great cost from sea snails, was the color of royalty. Wise, chakham, is used six times in the chapter, of Solomon and of the craftsmen alike: in Hebrew wisdom includes skill of hand.

The logs went by sea to Joppa, the nearest port to Jerusalem, and were hauled some thirty-five miles inland and uphill. English Bibles number this chapter differently from the Hebrew: English 2:1 is Hebrew 1:18.
passages.later: The law said of the foreigner, ‘You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt’ (Leviticus 19:34). Jeremiah later said, “Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness, and his upper rooms without justice, who makes his countrymen serve without pay” (Jeremiah 22:13).
passages.hard:
Were Solomon's builders forced labor, and does the Bible approve of it?

Verses 17 and 18 describe Solomon counting the foreigners in the land and setting them to work. First Kings 9 and 2 Chronicles 8 say these were descendants of the Canaanite peoples and that Israelites were not made slaves. Yet 1 Kings 5 also describes a levy of 30,000 Israelites sent to Lebanon in shifts, and 1 Kings 12 shows that Solomon's heavy yoke was the grievance that split the kingdom after his death. The Bible itself records the burden and its cost.

Compulsory state labor was standard in the ancient world, and the text reports it rather than commends it. The law of Moses calls Israel again and again to remember its own slavery in Egypt and to treat foreigners justly, and the word for foreigner here, ger, is the same word. The prophets later condemned kings who built with unpaid labor. The Chronicler, intent on the temple, does not stop to criticize, but the wider biblical story does, and chapter 10 will show the price.
passages.asks: The temple was built by skilled friends and by conscripted strangers. Ask who does the hidden, heavy work behind the things you enjoy, and whether they are treated justly. And ask whether anything you are building for God is being built on someone else's back.
